title: Terahertz nanoscopy of quantum-geometric photovoltaics in bilayer graphene
authors: Bogdan Borodin, Jiangxu Li, Xuanpu Zhang, Aleksei Karaborchev, Som Subhra Guria, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Roshan Krishna Kumar, Fan Zhang, Petr Stepanov
abstract: The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) provides a direct link between quantum geometry and nonlinear light-matter interactions, yet conventional far-field measurements cannot disentangle BPVE from contact- and interface-induced photothermoelectric signals. Here we develop cryogenic, polarization-sensitive terahertz microscopy with deep-subwavelength resolution and apply it to dual-gated AB bilayer graphene. Near resonance between the band gap and terahertz photon energy, we observe enhanced optical conductivity and spatially resolved BPVE. Polarization-dependent measurements reveal a characteristic twofold angular symmetry and a distinct shift-vector direction, both governed by crystalline symmetries and quantum geometry. The evolution of BPVE with carrier density and temperature provides a sensitive probe of the fine electronic structure of bilayer graphene, revealing signatures of trigonal warping and electron-hole asymmetry. Agreement with theory demonstrates that the terahertz nanoscopy of BPVE established here offers an optical lens into the interplay between band and quantum geometry in quantum materials.
summary: This work pioneers the use of cryogenic, polarization-sensitive terahertz nanoscopy to measure the Bulk Photovoltaic Effect (BPVE) in bilayer graphene. By employing near-field techniques, the authors successfully disentangle the intrinsic quantum-geometric photovoltaic signal from background photothermoelectric noise. This provides an optical lens into the fundamental interplay between band structure and quantum geometry in advanced 2D materials.
main_problem: To develop a technique to spatially and spectroscopically separate the intrinsic Bulk Photovoltaic Effect (BPVE) from confounding contact- and interface-induced photothermoelectric signals.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrated the nanoscale mapping of the BPVE in bilayer graphene, confirming its dependence on quantum geometry and revealing signatures of electronic structure details like trigonal warping.
method: The authors employed cryogenic, polarization-sensitive terahertz microscopy, specifically utilizing near-field scanning optical microscopy (s-SNOM) to achieve deep-subwavelength spatial resolution.
model_or_system: The physical system is dual-gated AB bilayer graphene, whose electronic properties are governed by quantum geometry, linking the BPVE to nonlinear light-matter interactions.
key_observables: Spatially resolved local photovoltage amplitude ($V_{ph}$), polarization-dependent photovoltage ($\propto \cos(2	heta - \phi)$), and the evolution of BPVE with carrier density ($n$) and displacement field ($D$).
important_parameters: Terahertz photon energy ($\hbar\omega \approx 10.5 	ext{ meV}$), cryogenic temperature ($12 	ext{ K}$), and the characteristic twofold angular symmetry.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on separating the intrinsic bulk response from extrinsic contributions, which is achieved by modeling the polarization dependence using an extraction anisotropy function.
figures_summary: Figures show the device architecture and far-field THz measurements, followed by near-field maps showing photovoltage vs. (n, D), and polarization dependence plots illustrating the separation of PTE, detected BPVE, and reconstructed intrinsic BPVE.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for advanced measurement techniques (far-field limitations) to implementing near-field s-SNOM measurements. It then details the rigorous polarization-resolved analysis to mathematically decompose the total signal into its intrinsic BPVE, PTE, and geometric coupling components.
why_interesting: The ability to optically probe quantum geometric effects like the BPVE at the nanoscale using THz spectroscopy provides a powerful, non-equilibrium tool for characterizing band structure and symmetry in 2D materials.

Figure 3d shows the power dependence of the observed BPVE. The black symbols denote the photovoltage am- plitude, which increases nearly linearly with excitation power, as expected for a second-order nonlinear effect. The red symbols denote the power-normalized photovolt- age amplitude. Although this quantity would be expected to remain constant, we observe a weak decrease with in- creasing excitation power. We attribute this deviation to photo-induced electron heating. The strong near-field enhancement at the s-SNOM tip, which can amplify the local electric field by a factor of 10–100, can induce lo- cal electron heating even at low incident powers.
